beats.trigger: ## From Personal to Team
beats.got: nothing new yet, but this is the part I care about: getting it out to non-engineers

beats.trigger: You can't really share an agent. You share its context, a skill, its output or an interface, and the choice between them is a strategy decision.
beats.got: sharing an agent breaks down into four different things, and picking one is a decision, not a copy-paste

beats.trigger: Bring one example from your own organisation of a tool people were given access to and then did not use.
beats.got: nothing new. I already have a few of these, our internal wiki bot is one

beats.trigger: **Draft** a technical plan and a people plan side by side
beats.got: nothing new, it's a list of verbs. the people plan part is what I usually skip

beats.trigger: What would you want a teammate to actually have: your folder, one of your skills, the output on a schedule, or a way to ask it a question in Slack?
beats.got: a concrete choice between folder, skill, schedule and slack bot. I'd have said slack bot before thinking

beats.trigger: That question is builder-centered and skips the one thing that decides whether sharing works: **the job** your teammate is trying to get done.
beats.got: start from the teammate's job, not from my build. fair, but I've heard JTBD before

beats.trigger: Read `module-7/jtbd.md`. The test is specificity: does it name one teammate, their current way of doing the job, and an outcome you could observe?
beats.got: agent reads my files and guesses a teammate's job. I pasted the prompt, glanced at the file and moved on. the 'read it and check' part felt like ceremony

beats.trigger: *"Share the whole agent"* is a vendor pitch and is NOT on the list.
beats.got: a clean four-way split of sharing: context, skill, push, pull. push vs pull is useful for sales, they won't run an agent themselves

beats.trigger: You now have the teammate's job and a candidate selected against it.
beats.got: nothing new, just a handover to the next exercise

beats.trigger: Now find the obstacle that decides whether the teammate can actually absorb it, then draft both halves of the plan.
beats.got: nothing new, setup for the next step

beats.trigger: The obstacle is usually not the first technical limitation a builder sees.
beats.got: the real blocker is usually social or political, not technical. that's me: I always go for the tech limit first

beats.trigger: A polished technical file beside a people file full of unnamed roles is the finding, not a finished rollout.
beats.got: my plans would look exactly like that, a great technical file and an empty people file. it stung a bit

beats.trigger: [Test the sharing plan](test-the-sharing-plan.md) checks the assumptions underneath these plans
beats.got: nothing new, a pointer to the next exercise

beats.trigger: The technical and people plans are hypotheses.
beats.got: nothing new. the plans are guesses to test

beats.trigger: *what would have to be true for this teammate, doing this job, to fire their current hire and use my candidate?*
beats.got: a way to ask why someone would switch, where I'd normally ask how to get them to. a good question to ask about the sales setup

beats.trigger: Six months from now, the teammate went back to the incumbent.
beats.got: a premortem on the rollout, ending in one named person and one question. usable, though I'd have wanted to go bigger than one person

beats.trigger: A candidate picked because it fits the infrastructure is shopping. A candidate picked because it moves the outcome is design.
beats.got: I've been shopping. my weekend sales setup was picked because I have the platform

beats.trigger: Whether they do gets settled outside the files, in their week.
beats.got: nothing new, a framing line before the lecture

beats.trigger: The fourth does not copy at all, which is why the product being sold as a shared agent is always three of the four parts, with the fourth still sitting with whoever built it.
beats.got: context, boundary and checks copy, but accountability stays with the builder. that is my who-maintains-this problem, now it has a name

beats.trigger: The two get reported as one number and they are not one thing.
beats.got: seat counts say nothing about use. we report licences, not usage

beats.trigger: The proposal got neither a yes nor a no.
beats.got: a real story of agents doing the analysis well and nobody deciding. I've seen engineering proposals die like that

beats.trigger: A teammate absorbs a skill or an output when it fits a job they already have and someone they trust has used it.
beats.got: someone they trust has to use it first. fine, but I'm not the trusted one for sales

beats.trigger: Your candidate is not competing with nothing. It is competing with that.
beats.got: my sales setup competes with their spreadsheets and habits, not with nothing

beats.trigger: Ask them how they do the job today, and listen before you show them anything.
beats.got: talk to one person before building. sensible, but slower than I'd like

beats.got: next module is agents building agents, which is the one I actually want

take_homes: the accountability part of an agent doesn't copy. whoever builds it still answers for it, and that's my maintenance problem with the sales setup
ask what job the teammate is trying to get done, and what would make them switch, before I build anything for them. don't start with what I built
access isn't uptake. I should measure who actually uses what I roll out, not who has a seat

monday.move: talk to the head of sales about how they do pipeline reviews today. I won't show the setup until they've finished talking. I'll check whether anyone besides me would own it
monday.who: head of sales (name stays unassigned until I ask)
monday.stop_condition: if nobody in sales wants it or will own it, I stop building it. if I find myself demoing before they've finished, I stop and ask more
monday.blocker: nobody in sales asked for it and I haven't checked who maintains it. also I'll want to build first and ask later

misconception.why: the module is about whether people take things up, not whether output is right. I skipped every read-and-check step and nothing stopped me or showed a cost. the accountability slide and the stalled-proposal story were closest, but they left me thinking about maintenance and trust, not checking my own output. 'checking is for beginners' is still intact.

one_line: good for the non-engineering rollout problem, the 'accountability doesn't copy' idea alone was worth it. a bit slow and ceremonial in the middle, and I skipped half the review steps without anything bad happening.
